newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysian stocks fall sharply on foreign sales.
newsitem.headline: Malaysian stocks fall sharply on foreign sales.

text.p: Share prices on the Kuala Lumpur Stock Exchange fell sharply on Monday morning on selling by foreigners, analysts and brokers said.
They said today's selling, part of a continuing exodus of funds from Malaysia, was mainly due to a sharp decline in the ringgit's value against the U.S. dollar.
At the lunch break, the benchmark Kuala Lumpur Stock Exchange Composite Index was down 2.84 perecnt or 26.49 points to 905.87.
Dealers said share prices fell across the board with losers swamping gainers, 667 stocks to 42. But volume was thin at 103 million shares valued at 548 million ringgit ($200.7 million).
"U.S. hedge funds are continuing to get out of the ringgit instruments and that is hurting stocks," said an associate director of research at a foreign brokerage in Kuala Lumpur.

The ringgit fell to a 42-month low of 2.7300 at around 0430 GMT from around 2.6850 in early morning trading. The decline followed comments by Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad on Friday that Malaysia was happy with the ringgit's level.
"It is only the currency factor today. The uncertainty surrounding the ringgit is really serious," the research director said.

"Now the CI (Composite Index) will test 900 soon. But the bottom does not look too far off -- give it another 20 points, maybe at 880, there should be a rebound," said an institutional dealer at a bank-backed brokerage.
Other dealers said they would rather not make a forecast as the index has passed previous support levels without a pause.
"What I am surprised at is local funds have not come in to support the market," one analyst said.
"I would have expected greater support from local funds after Mahathir's comments last week," he said.
Mahathir on Thursday said he expected local funds to start buying. On Friday, the funds complied, helping the index recover slightly.
"It has become a major concern that the currency is being hit so severely," said the head of research at a foreign brokerage.
"While all the stocks are getting cheaper everyday, people are looking at whether or not there is a macroeconomic problem that needs to be addressed (in Malaysia)," he said.
Some lower-than-expected corporate results -- including blue chips Telekom and Genting with Proton predicting lower profit growth -- have added to the gloomy sentiment.
"Another piece of bad news is that the Bakun listing is being delayed," said a dealer with a bank-backed brokerage.

The Bakun Hydroelectric Corporation, the operator of the $6.18 billion project to generate 2,400 MW of power, is planning to issue 1.5 billion shares at two ringgit each, the biggest-ever public issue in Malaysia's history.
Minister of Energy, Posts and Telecommunications Leo Moggie said on Monday the listing could be delayed due to a dispute between Ekran and Asea Brown Boveri, the two main contractors.
